source.text: כִּ֛י נַ֥עַר יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וָאֹהֲבֵ֑הוּ וּמִמִּצְרַ֖יִם קָרָ֥אתִי לִבְנִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: When [was] a youth Israel, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called to my son.

en.L: When Israel [was] a boy, I loved him, \q and out of Egypt I called {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} son.
en.B: When Israel was a boy, I loved him, \q and out of Egypt I called {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} son.
en.R: When Israel was a child, I loved him. \q I called {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} son out of Egypt.

pt.L: Quando Israel [era] um menino, eu o amei, \q e do Egito chamei o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} filho.
pt.B: Eu amei Israel quando ele era menino, \q e do Egito chamei o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} filho.
pt.R: Quando Israel era criança, eu o amei. \q Eu chamei o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} filho para fora do Egito.

decisions.choice: out of Egypt I called my son: the exodus, quoted in Matthew 2:15
alternatives: a prediction about the Messiah only
decisions.reason: The son is Israel, the people God brought out of Egypt; God had told Pharaoh, "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22-23). Hosea looks back on the exodus as the start of a father's love. Matthew 2:15 quotes these words of Jesus, God's Son, who went down into Egypt and came out again, living through Israel's story himself. Matthew's words agree with the Hebrew here ("my son"); the Greek translation of Hosea reads "his children", so Matthew did not take the line from it. This description of the Greek is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: a boy, a child: Israel's earliest days as a people, in Egypt and at the exodus
decisions.reason: The word covers a boy from infancy to youth. Hosea pictures the nation's beginnings as a childhood, as he speaks of "the days of her youth" when Israel came up from Egypt (2:17). Verses 3-4 go on with the picture: a parent teaching a small child to walk and stooping to feed it.

decisions.choice: I loved him: love that came first, before Israel had done anything
decisions.reason: God's love is the starting point of the chapter. It was not earned: the LORD set his love on Israel when they were a small and enslaved people (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). The rest of the chapter weighs this love against Israel's turning away (verses 2-7) and ends with love winning out (verses 8-11).

decisions.choice: I called my son out of Egypt: God summoned his son to leave Egypt
alternatives: ever since Egypt I have called my son (compare 12:10; 13:4, "from the land of Egypt")
decisions.reason: The verb "call" takes a small word "to" before "my son", as calling often does in Hebrew. Read with "out of Egypt", it is the summons of the exodus. Verse 2 picks up the same verb: God called, and others called, but Israel went the other way.

decisions.choice: Out of Egypt I called my son (L, B); I called my son out of Egypt (R)
alternatives: Out of Egypt I called to my son
decisions.reason: Each level uses the same words for this line as Open Word Bible's Matthew 2:15 at that level, so a reader can see the quotation (m1). Literal does not show the small word "to", since English "call" needs no word before its object; the meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: my son (deity pronoun setting on "my")
decisions.reason: God is speaking, so "my" takes the deity pronoun setting, as it does in Matthew 2:15. "Him" and "son" refer to Israel and take no setting.

decisions.choice: do Egito chamei o meu filho (L, B); Eu chamei o meu filho para fora do Egito (R)
alternatives: do Egito chamei a meu filho
decisions.reason: Matthew 2:15 quotes this line, and the Hebrew and the Greek agree, so each level uses the Portuguese words of Matthew 2:15 at the same level (r-en-1), with the deity_pronoun span on "meu" as there (r-en-2). The first line, one of Hosea's best-known, is drafted from the Hebrew away from the familiar versions; Balanced puts God's love first.

source.text: קָרְא֖וּ לָהֶ֑ם כֵּ֚ן הָלְכ֣וּ מִפְּנֵיהֶ֔ם לַבְּעָלִ֣ים יְזַבֵּ֔חוּ וְלַפְּסִלִ֖ים יְקַטֵּרֽוּן׃

records.literal_gloss: They called to them; so they went from before them; to the Baals they sacrificed, and to the carved images they made smoke.

en.L: They called to them; \q so they went away from them. \q To the Baals they sacrificed, \q and to the carved images they burned offerings.
en.B: The more they called to them, \q the more they went away from them. \q They sacrificed to the Baals \q and burned offerings to carved idols.
en.R: The more the prophets called to Israel, \q the more the people turned away. \q They offered sacrifices to the Baals \q and burned offerings to idols.

pt.L: Chamavam-nos; \q assim eles se afastavam deles. \q Aos baalins sacrificavam, \q e às imagens esculpidas queimavam ofertas.
pt.B: Quanto mais os chamavam, \q mais eles se afastavam deles. \q Ofereciam sacrifícios aos baalins \q e queimavam ofertas a ídolos esculpidos.
pt.R: Quanto mais os profetas chamavam Israel, \q mais o povo se afastava. \q Eles ofereciam sacrifícios aos baalins \q e queimavam ofertas a ídolos.

decisions.choice: They called to them ... away from them: messengers called Israel, and Israel walked away from them
alternatives: As I called them, so they went away from me (the reading of the Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "they called", most naturally the prophets and other messengers God sent (12:11; 2 Kings 17:13), and Israel went away from them. The Greek translation reads "as I called them, so they went away from me", which continues God's own calling from verse 1; the difference is a matter of a few letters. The Hebrew text is followed. This description of the Greek is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: so they went: the more they were called, the more they went away
decisions.reason: "So" sets the going away against the calling as its match: each call was answered by more distance.

decisions.choice: the Baals and carved images: the gods of Canaan and the idols that stood for them
decisions.reason: Baal was the Canaanite storm god, believed to give rain and harvest. "The Baals" are the local forms of his worship at many shrines (2:15, 19). Carved images were idols shaped from wood or stone, or cast and then shaped (8:4-6; 13:2).

decisions.choice: burned offerings: made sacrifices go up in smoke
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something go up in smoke. It is used for burning incense and for burning the parts of a sacrifice on the altar (4:13). Here it stands beside "sacrificed" for the whole of the worship given to idols.

decisions.choice: the prophets ... the people (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names who called and who turned away, so that the two "they"s are not confused. It follows the reading chosen in m1; the Hebrew itself does not name the callers.

decisions.choice: The more ... the more (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "the more ... the more" to make plain how each call was matched by more distance (m2).

source.text: וְאָנֹכִ֤י תִרְגַּ֨לְתִּי֙ לְאֶפְרַ֔יִם קָחָ֖ם עַל־זְרֽוֹעֹתָ֑יו וְלֹ֥א יָדְע֖וּ כִּ֥י רְפָאתִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And I, I taught to walk Ephraim, taking them by his arms; and not they knew that I healed them.

en.L: And I, I taught Ephraim to walk, \q taking them by his arms, \q but they did not know that I healed them.
en.B: Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, \q holding them by the arms, \q but they did not know that I was the one who healed them.
en.R: I was the one who taught Ephraim to walk. \q I held them by the arms. \q But they did not know that I was the one who healed them.

pt.L: E eu, eu ensinei Efraim a andar, \q tomando-os pelos seus braços, \q mas eles não souberam que eu os curava.
pt.B: No entanto, quem ensinou Efraim a dar os primeiros passos fui eu, \q segurando-os pelos braços, \q mas eles não reconheceram que era eu quem os curava.
pt.R: Fui eu que ensinei Efraim a andar. \q Eu os segurava pelos braços. \q Mas eles não sabiam que era eu quem os curava.

decisions.choice: I taught Ephraim to walk: the patient care of a parent for a toddler
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for "foot" and is found only here. The picture of verse 1 goes on: God is the parent guiding the child's first steps. The stressed "I" sets God's care against Israel's going after the Baals (verse 2).

decisions.choice: taking them by his arms: the Hebrew as written, the parent holding the child up by the arms
alternatives: I took them up in my arms (the reading of the ancient translations)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew reads "taking them by his arms", that is, by Ephraim's arms, as a parent steadies a child learning to walk. The Greek, Syriac and Latin translations read "I took them up in my arms", which changes the person of two words. Both give the same picture of care. This description of the ancient translations is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: I healed them: the LORD as Israel's healer
decisions.reason: At the start of the wilderness journey the LORD said, "I am the LORD who heals you" (Exodus 15:26). Hosea often uses healing for God's restoring of his people (5:13; 6:1; 7:1; 14:5). Israel did not see whose care had kept them.

decisions.choice: Ephraim ... them: the people as one child and as many people
decisions.reason: Hosea moves between the singular (Ephraim, "him", "his") and the plural ("them") because Ephraim is both one son and a whole people.

decisions.choice: it was I who ... I was the one who (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew stresses "I" at the start and in "I healed them". Balanced and Readable carry the stress with "it was I who" and "I was the one who"; Literal repeats "I".

decisions.choice: ensinei Efraim a andar (L, R), a dar os primeiros passos (B); era eu quem os curava
decisions.reason: Verses 1-4 are among the best-known lines of Hosea in Portuguese, so they are drafted from the Hebrew and the gloss, away from the familiar versions' wording. The stressed "I" (r-en-1) is "eu, eu" at Literal, "quem ... fui eu" at Balanced and "Fui eu que" at Readable; "dar os primeiros passos" keeps the picture of a toddler (m1).

source.text: בְּחַבְלֵ֨י אָדָ֤ם אֶמְשְׁכֵם֙ בַּעֲבֹת֣וֹת אַהֲבָ֔ה וָאֶהְיֶ֥ה לָהֶ֛ם כִּמְרִ֥ימֵי עֹ֖ל עַ֣ל לְחֵיהֶ֑ם וְאַ֥ט אֵלָ֖יו אוֹכִֽיל׃

records.literal_gloss: With cords of a human I drew them, with ropes of love; and I was to them like those who lift a yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to him; I fed [him].

en.L: With cords of a human I drew them, with ropes of love, \q and I was to them like those who lift a yoke off their jaws, \q and I bent down to him [and] fed [him].
en.B: I led them with human cords, with ropes of love. \q To them I was like someone who lifts the yoke off their jaws, \q and I bent down to them and fed them.
en.R: I led them with cords of kindness, the kind used for people, with ropes of love. \q I was like someone who eases the yoke on an animal's jaws. \q I bent down to them and fed them.

pt.L: Com cordas de homem eu os puxava, com cordas de amor, \q e eu era para eles como os que erguem o jugo das suas mandíbulas, \q e me inclinava para ele [e o] alimentava.
pt.B: Eu os guiava com cordas próprias para pessoas, com cordas de amor. \q Para eles eu era como quem tira a canga das suas mandíbulas, \q e me abaixei até eles e os alimentei.
pt.R: Eu os guiei com cordas de bondade, do tipo usado para pessoas, com cordas de amor. \q Eu era como alguém que afrouxa a canga no queixo de um animal. \q Eu me abaixei até eles e dei comida a eles.

decisions.choice: cords of a human, ropes of love: God led Israel by gentle means fit for people, not by force
decisions.reason: "Cords of a human" are cords suited to human beings, set beside "ropes of love". God did not drive Israel like a beast but drew them with kindness. The words prepare for the picture that follows, where the cords that might bind an animal are loosened.

decisions.choice: like those who lift a yoke off their jaws: a farmer easing the yoke so that the animal can eat
alternatives: like those who lift an infant to their cheeks (a reading that changes only the vowels of the word for "yoke")
decisions.reason: As the Hebrew is written, God is like a farmer who loosens or raises the yoke from an ox's jaws, so that it can rest and feed; "I bent down and fed him" then follows naturally. With different vowels, the same letters can mean "infant", giving the picture of a parent lifting a baby to the cheek, which suits verses 1 and 3. The written vowels are followed; the line is uncertain.

decisions.choice: I bent down to him and fed him: God stooping to feed his people
decisions.reason: The word read as "I bent down" may also be read as "gently". Either way God stoops to feed the one he leads. "Him" is Ephraim as one person, the child of verse 1. The feeding recalls the manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16).

decisions.choice: cords of kindness, the kind used for people ... an animal's jaws (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "cords of a human" means (m1) and makes clear that the yoke picture is about a working animal (m2). It follows the reading chosen in m2.

decisions.choice: [and] fed [him] (L)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has two verbs side by side, "I bent down to him, I fed", with no "and" and no object; Literal brackets both.

decisions.choice: to them ... fed them (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "him" for Ephraim as one person (m3). Balanced and Readable say "them", as in the first half of the verse, so the reader does not look for a new person.

decisions.choice: cordas de homem (L), cordas próprias para pessoas (B), cordas de bondade, do tipo usado para pessoas (R); o jugo (L), a canga (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Cords of a human" are cords fit for people, not for animals (m1); Literal keeps the Hebrew noun, and Balanced and Readable say what it means, away from the familiar wording. The yoke on a working animal is "a canga", the farm word Brazilians use for it, at Balanced and Readable, as in 10:10-11; Literal keeps "jugo".

source.text: לֹ֤א יָשׁוּב֙ אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם וְאַשּׁ֖וּר ה֣וּא מַלְכּ֑וֹ כִּ֥י מֵאֲנ֖וּ לָשֽׁוּב׃

records.literal_gloss: Not he will return to [the] land of Egypt, and Assyria, he [will be] his king, for they refused to return.

en.L: He will not return to the land of Egypt, \q but Assyria, he [will be] his king, \q because they refused to return.
en.B: He will not go back to the land of Egypt; \q Assyria will be his king instead, \q because they refused to return to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.R: They will not go back to Egypt. \q Instead, the king of Assyria will rule over them, \q because they refused to come back to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

pt.L: Ele não voltará à terra do Egito, \q mas a Assíria, ela [será] o seu rei, \q porque recusaram voltar.
pt.B: Ele não voltará à terra do Egito; \q a Assíria será o seu rei, \q porque recusaram voltar para {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}.
pt.R: Eles não vão voltar para o Egito. \q Em vez disso, o rei da Assíria vai governá-los, \q porque se recusaram a voltar para {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}.

decisions.choice: He will not return to Egypt: Egypt will be no refuge; Assyria will rule him
alternatives: He will return to Egypt (reading the first word as "to him" and joining it to verse 4, as 8:13 and 9:3 say)
a question: Will he not return to the land of Egypt?
decisions.reason: As written, the verse says that Ephraim will not go back to Egypt, the land of its slavery and the power it looked to for help (7:11; 12:2); Assyria will be its master instead. Hosea also says that "they will return to Egypt" (8:13; 9:3), so some read the first word, which sounds the same as "to him", as the end of verse 4, or take the line as a question. The words as written are followed.

decisions.choice: return ... refused to return: a play on the verb "turn back"
decisions.reason: The same verb is used twice. Ephraim will not turn back to Egypt, because it would not turn back to God. To "return" is Hosea's word for repentance (3:5; 6:1; 14:2).

decisions.choice: Assyria will be his king: the northern kingdom under Assyrian rule
decisions.reason: The last kings of Israel paid tribute to Assyria, and when King Hoshea turned to Egypt for help, Assyria took Samaria and carried the people away (2 Kings 17:3-6), in 722 BC.

decisions.choice: return to me (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whom Israel refused to return to, which the Hebrew leaves implied (m2). God is the speaker, so "me" takes the deity pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: the king of Assyria will rule over them (R)
decisions.reason: Readable puts the picture of a nation as king into plain words, and uses "they" for Ephraim, as it does through the chapter.

source.text: וְחָלָ֥ה חֶ֨רֶב֙ בְּעָרָ֔יו וְכִלְּתָ֥ה בַדָּ֖יו וְאָכָ֑לָה מִֽמֹּעֲצ֖וֹתֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And will whirl [the] sword in his cities, and will finish his bars, and will devour, because of their counsels.

en.L: And the sword will whirl in his cities \q and put an end to his bars and devour [them], \q because of their schemes.
en.B: A sword will sweep through their cities; \q it will break the bars of their gates and consume them, \q because of their own schemes.
en.R: Swords will sweep through their cities. \q They will smash the bars of their gates and destroy the people, \q because of the plans they made.

pt.L: E a espada rodopiará nas suas cidades \q e acabará com as suas trancas e [as] devorará, \q por causa dos seus planos.
pt.B: Uma espada varrerá as suas cidades; \q quebrará as trancas das suas portas e os consumirá, \q por causa dos seus próprios planos.
pt.R: Espadas vão varrer as suas cidades. \q Vão quebrar as trancas das portas e destruir o povo, \q por causa dos planos que eles fizeram.

decisions.choice: his bars: the bars that bolt the city gates
alternatives: his empty talkers (the same letters form a word for boasters or false prophets, Isaiah 44:25; Jeremiah 50:36)
decisions.reason: The word can mean the bars or poles that bolt a gate (Job 17:16; compare Job 18:13), which suits a sword raging through cities. The same letters also spell a word for idle talkers or diviners, which would fit "their schemes". The first sense is followed.

decisions.choice: the sword will whirl: war will rage through the land
decisions.reason: The verb means to whirl or to writhe. The sword, standing for an invading army, swings and flashes as it goes through the cities.

decisions.choice: their schemes: the plans they made, above all their alliances
decisions.reason: The word means counsel or plans. Ephraim's leaders schemed to save themselves by treaties with Egypt and Assyria (7:11; 12:2), and the plans themselves bring the sword.

decisions.choice: the bars of their gates ... consume them (B); destroy the people (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the bars are (m1) and supply the object of "devour". They use "their" for Ephraim's "his", since the people are meant.

source.text: וְעַמִּ֥י תְלוּאִ֖ים לִמְשֽׁוּבָתִ֑י וְאֶל־עַל֙ יִקְרָאֻ֔הוּ יַ֖חַד לֹ֥א יְרוֹמֵם׃

records.literal_gloss: And my people [are] hung on turning from me; and to [the] height they call him; together not he lifts up.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} people are bent on turning away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; \q and to [the One] on high they call him, \q [but] none at all rises up.
en.B: My people are set on turning away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q Though they are called to the One on high, \q not one of them rises up.
en.R: My people are determined to turn away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q They are called to come up to God Most High, \q but not one of them gets up to come.

pt.L: E o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} povo está decidido a se afastar de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}; \q e para [Aquele que está no] alto o chamam, \q [mas] ninguém se levanta.
pt.B: O {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} povo está decidido a se afastar de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}. \q Ainda que sejam chamados para Aquele que está no alto, \q nenhum deles se levanta.
pt.R: O {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} povo está decidido a se afastar de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}. \q Eles são chamados a subir até o Deus Altíssimo, \q mas nenhum deles se levanta para vir.

decisions.choice: hung on: fixed on, set on
decisions.reason: The verb means to hang or to be hung. Here it pictures a people whose hearts are hung on, fixed on, turning away. It is used in Deuteronomy 28:66 of a life that "hangs in doubt", so some take it as wavering; the next lines suggest a settled refusal.

decisions.choice: turning away from me: unfaithfulness to God
decisions.reason: The noun comes from the verb "turn", like "return" in verse 5. Hosea uses it of Israel's backsliding, and God promises to heal it (14:5; compare Jeremiah 3:22).

decisions.choice: they are called upward, to the One on high, but not one of them rises: the people will not answer the call
alternatives: they call to the Most High, but he will not raise them up at all
they call him to a false god (reading the word for "on high" as a name)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew of this line is among the hardest in the book, and every translation is a guess. "They call him" most likely continues verse 2, where messengers called Israel. The word for "on high" is the one in 7:16, "they turn, but not upward", and here may mean God Most High. The last words, "together he does not lift up", are taken as "not one rises". Taken another way, the line says that the people call to God but he will not lift them up.

decisions.choice: they are called (B, R); gets up to come (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "they are called", since the callers are the messengers of verse 2 and the one called is Israel. Readable puts "does not lift up" as not getting up to come. Both follow the reading chosen in m3.

source.text: אֵ֞יךְ אֶתֶּנְךָ֣ אֶפְרַ֗יִם אֲמַגֶּנְךָ֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵ֚יךְ אֶתֶּנְךָ֣ כְאַדְמָ֔ה אֲשִֽׂימְךָ֖ כִּצְבֹאיִ֑ם נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ עָלַי֙ לִבִּ֔י יַ֖חַד נִכְמְר֥וּ נִחוּמָֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: How will I give you up, Ephraim? [How] will I hand you over, Israel? How will I make you like Admah? [How] will I set you like Zeboiim? Is turned over within me my heart; together are kindled my compassions.

en.L: How can I give you up, Ephraim? [How can] I surrender you, Israel? \q How can I treat you like Admah? \q [How can] I set you like Zeboiim? \q My heart is turned over within {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; \q all together {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} compassion grows warm.
en.B: How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I surrender you, Israel? \q How can I treat you like Admah? \q How can I make you like Zeboiim? \q Within {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} heart turns over; \q all {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} compassion is stirred.
en.R: Ephraim, how can I give you up? Israel, how can I hand you over to your enemies? \q How can I destroy you as I destroyed Admah? \q How can I treat you like Zeboiim? Those towns were wiped out with Sodom. \q My heart is turned upside down within {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. \q All {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} tender love for you is stirred up.

pt.L: Como te entregarei, Efraim? [Como] te abandonarei, Israel? \q Como te tratarei como Admá? \q [Como] te porei como Zeboim? \q O {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} coração se revolve dentro de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}; \q todas juntas, as {{deity_pronoun:minhas|Minhas}} compaixões se aquecem.
pt.B: Como posso te abandonar, Efraim? Como posso te entregar, Israel? \q Como posso te tratar como Admá? \q Como posso fazer de ti o que fiz a Zeboim? \q Dentro de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}} o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} coração se revira; \q toda a {{deity_pronoun:minha|Minha}} compaixão se comove.
pt.R: Efraim, como posso desistir de ti? Israel, como posso te entregar aos teus inimigos? \q Como posso te destruir como destruí Admá? \q Como posso te tratar como Zeboim? Essas cidades foram destruídas junto com Sodoma. \q O {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} coração está revirado dentro de {{deity_pronoun:mim|Mim}}. \q Todo o {{deity_pronoun:meu|Meu}} terno amor por ti está comovido.

decisions.choice: Admah and Zeboiim: the cities destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah
decisions.reason: Admah and Zeboiim were cities of the plain, named with Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 10:19; 14:2) and destroyed with them (Genesis 19:24-25). Deuteronomy 29:22 names all four as the picture of the curse that would fall on Israel if it broke the covenant: a land burned out "like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim". Hosea names the two lesser cities. Ephraim deserves their fate, and God asks how he can give it.

decisions.choice: my heart is turned over: the same verb as the "overthrow" of those cities
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the overthrow of Sodom and the other cities (Genesis 19:25; Deuteronomy 29:22). Instead of overturning Ephraim, God's own heart is overturned. The heart is the seat of thought and will, so the words describe a change of purpose as well as deep feeling.

decisions.choice: my compassion grows warm: tender love stirred to its depths
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used of Joseph, whose "compassion grew warm" for his brother (Genesis 43:30), and of the mother who would rather lose her son than see him killed (1 Kings 3:26). The word for compassion is related to the word for womb. God's love for Ephraim is the love of a parent for a child.

decisions.choice: How can I ...? Questions of anguish, not of doubt about God's power
decisions.reason: God is able to give Ephraim up, and Ephraim deserves it (verses 5-7). The questions say how much it costs God to think of it. Verse 9 gives the answer: he will not.

decisions.choice: [How can] (L); How can (B)
decisions.reason: In the Hebrew, "how" is written only before the first and third questions and carries over to the second and fourth. Literal brackets the words carried over; Balanced repeats them.

decisions.choice: hand you over to your enemies ... destroy you as I destroyed Admah ... Those towns were wiped out with Sodom (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom Ephraim would be handed over, what being made like Admah would mean, and who Admah and Zeboiim were (m1), so that a reader who does not know the names can follow.

decisions.choice: compassion (L, B); tender love (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew noun is plural, a common way of speaking of deep feelings. English says "compassion". Readable says "tender love" to keep the warmth of the word (m3).

decisions.choice: Admá, Zeboim
decisions.reason: The cities destroyed with Sodom (m1) take the forms Deuteronomy 29:22 gives them in Portuguese, "Admá e Zeboim"; Readable says who they were, as the English Readable does (r-en-2). God speaks to Ephraim and Israel as one, with "tu".

decisions.choice: se revolve (L), se revira (B), está revirado (R); compaixões (L), compaixão (B), terno amor (R)
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the overthrow of Sodom (m2); Portuguese cannot keep the same verb for both, so it keeps the picture of the heart turned over, "revolver-se", "revirar-se". The plural "compaixões" stands at Literal, as the Hebrew has it; Balanced says "compaixão", the noun of the names in 1:6, and Readable "terno amor", as the English (r-en-3). God's "meu" takes the deity_pronoun span, as elsewhere in the book.

source.text: לֹ֤א אֶֽעֱשֶׂה֙ חֲר֣וֹן אַפִּ֔י לֹ֥א אָשׁ֖וּב לְשַׁחֵ֣ת אֶפְרָ֑יִם כִּ֣י אֵ֤ל אָֽנֹכִי֙ וְלֹא־אִ֔ישׁ בְּקִרְבְּךָ֣ קָד֔וֹשׁ וְלֹ֥א אָב֖וֹא בְּעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: Not I will carry out [the] burning of my anger; not I will return to destroy Ephraim; for God I [am] and not a man, in your midst [the] Holy One, and not I will come in wrath.

en.L: I will not carry out the burning of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} anger; \q I will not again destroy Ephraim; \q for I [am] God and not {{gender:a human|a man}}, \q the Holy One in your midst, \q and I will not come in wrath.
en.B: I will not act on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} burning anger; \q I will not turn to destroy Ephraim again. \q For I am God and not {{gender:a human|a man}}, \q the Holy One among you, \q and I will not come in fury.
en.R: I will not let {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fierce anger loose on you. \q I will not destroy Ephraim again. \q I am God, not a human being. \q I am the Holy One who lives among you. \q I will not come to you in anger.

pt.L: Não executarei o ardor da {{deity_pronoun:minha|Minha}} ira; \q não voltarei a destruir Efraim; \q porque eu [sou] Deus e não {{gender:um ser humano|um homem}}, \q o Santo no meio de ti, \q e não virei com furor.
pt.B: Não agirei segundo o ardor da {{deity_pronoun:minha|Minha}} ira; \q não tornarei a destruir Efraim. \q Pois eu sou Deus e não {{gender:um ser humano|um homem}}, \q o Santo no meio de ti, \q e não virei com fúria.
pt.R: Não vou soltar contra ti a {{deity_pronoun:minha|Minha}} ira ardente. \q Não vou destruir Efraim de novo. \q Eu sou Deus, não um ser humano. \q Eu sou o Santo que vive no meio de ti. \q Não vou chegar a ti com ira.

decisions.choice: I am God and not a man: God's holiness shows itself in mercy
decisions.reason: A human being in such anger would strike, and Ephraim has earned it. God is not bound to act as people do. Being God, "the Holy One", wholly other than humans, is the reason he holds back. The same contrast is used in Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29, where it says that God does not lie or change his mind as people do; here it says that he will not destroy as people would.

decisions.choice: a man: a human being, set against God
decisions.reason: The word usually means a man. Set against "God", it means any human being, man or woman, as in Numbers 23:19. The point is the difference between God and humankind, not between God and men.

decisions.choice: I will not again destroy: there will be no second Admah
alternatives: I will not turn back to destroy ("turn" meaning a change of course)
decisions.reason: The verb "return" is often used to mean "do again". God will not repeat the overthrow of verse 8 on Ephraim. It can also mean that God will not turn around to destroy. Either way the threat of verse 8 is withdrawn.

decisions.choice: in wrath
alternatives: into a city (the same letters spell the common word for "city")
decisions.reason: The last word can be read as "in wrath", matching "the burning of my anger" at the start of the verse, or as "into a city", as if God would not come to destroy a city. The first reading is followed.

decisions.choice: not a human (L, B, with "a man" as the gender setting's alternative); not a human being (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew means a human being here (m2), so Literal and Balanced use the gender setting, with the inclusive word as the default and the traditional "a man" as the alternative, as Numbers 23:19 does. Readable says "a human being", which is already inclusive and needs no setting. God is never given a gender span.

decisions.choice: act on my burning anger (B); let my fierce anger loose on you (R)
alternatives: carry out the burning of my anger
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the Hebrew phrase in natural English; Literal keeps "carry out the burning of my anger".

decisions.choice: {{gender:um ser humano|um homem}}
decisions.reason: The word means any human being, set against God (m2), and Portuguese has two wordings, so Literal and Balanced take the gender setting, as the English does (r-en-1), with "um ser humano" by default; Readable says "um ser humano" plainly. "O Santo", God's title, is capitalised as Isaiah 1:4 has it; "no meio de ti", since the "you" is singular, Ephraim as one.

source.text: אַחֲרֵ֧י יְהוָ֛ה יֵלְכ֖וּ כְּאַרְיֵ֣ה יִשְׁאָ֑ג כִּֽי־ה֣וּא יִשְׁאַ֔ג וְיֶחֶרְד֥וּ בָנִ֖ים מִיָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: After Yahweh they will walk; like a lion he will roar; for he, he will roar, and will come trembling [the] children from [the] west.

en.L: After {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} they will walk; like a lion {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will roar; \q for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will roar, \q and {{gender:children|sons}} will come trembling from the west.
en.B: They will follow {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, who will roar like a lion. \q When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} roars, \q {{gender:children|sons}} will come trembling from the west.
en.R: The people will follow {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, who will roar like a lion. \q When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} roars, \q they will come back from the west, trembling.

pt.L: Atrás {{divine_name:do SENHOR|de Javé}} andarão; como um leão {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} rugirá; \q quando {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} rugir, \q filhos virão tremendo do ocidente.
pt.B: Eles seguirão {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}}, que rugirá como um leão. \q Quando {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} rugir, \q filhos virão tremendo do ocidente.
pt.R: O povo vai seguir {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}}, que vai rugir como um leão. \q Quando {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} rugir, \q eles vão voltar do ocidente, tremendo.

decisions.choice: they will walk after the LORD: the people will follow God; the prophet speaks of God for a moment
decisions.reason: To walk after someone is to follow and obey him (Deuteronomy 13:5). God, who has spoken as "I" through the chapter, is named here, and in verse 11 speaks as "I" again. Such changes of voice are common in the prophets.

decisions.choice: roar like a lion: here a call that brings the scattered home
decisions.reason: Elsewhere the lion's roar is a picture of judgment (5:14; 13:7; Amos 1:2; 3:8). Here the same roar is a summons: when God calls, his people come back.

decisions.choice: come trembling from the west: hurry home in awe, from across the sea
decisions.reason: The verb means to tremble, and with "from" it pictures people hurrying, shaken, as birds flutter (verse 11). "The west" is literally "the sea", the Mediterranean, which lies west of the land; the scattered will come back from every side.

decisions.choice: children, with "sons" as the gender setting's alternative (L, B); they (R)
decisions.reason: The word is "sons", meaning the people of Israel, men and women, so it takes the gender setting. Readable says "they" for the people named at the start of its sentence.

source.text: יֶחֶרְד֤וּ כְצִפּוֹר֙ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם וּכְיוֹנָ֖ה מֵאֶ֣רֶץ אַשּׁ֑וּר וְהוֹשַׁבְתִּ֥ים עַל־בָּתֵּיהֶ֖ם נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃ס

records.literal_gloss: They will come trembling like a bird from Egypt, and like a dove from [the] land of Assyria; and I will cause them to dwell in their houses, declaration of Yahweh.

en.L: They will come trembling like a bird from Egypt, \q and like a dove from the land of Assyria, \q and I will make them dwell in their houses, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: They will come trembling like birds from Egypt, \q like doves from the land of Assyria, \q and I will settle them in their homes, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: They will hurry back from Egypt, trembling like birds. \q They will come from Assyria like doves. \q I will let them live in their own homes again, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

pt.L: Virão tremendo como um pássaro do Egito, \q e como uma pomba da terra da Assíria, \q e os farei habitar nas suas casas, declara {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}}.
pt.B: Virão tremendo como pássaros do Egito, \q como pombas da terra da Assíria, \q e eu os farei morar nos seus lares, declara {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}}.
pt.R: Eles vão voltar depressa do Egito, tremendo como pássaros. \q Vão chegar da Assíria como pombas. \q Vou deixá-los morar de novo nas suas próprias casas, diz {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}}.

decisions.choice: like a bird ... like a dove from Egypt and Assyria: the foolish dove of 7:11 coming home
decisions.reason: In 7:11 Ephraim is "like a dove, silly and without sense", calling to Egypt and going to Assyria for help. The same two lands, and the same bird, return here. The people who flew to those powers will fly back from them.

decisions.choice: I will settle them in their houses: the exile undone
decisions.reason: The threat of verse 5 and of 9:3, that Ephraim would live in a foreign land, is reversed: God will bring them back to live in their own homes.

decisions.choice: declares the LORD: the end of the poem and of a section
decisions.reason: The formula closes the oracle, and the Hebrew text marks a section break after this verse. The next verse is 12:1 in the Hebrew text and 11:12 in many Bibles; see the note there.

decisions.choice: declares the LORD (L, B); says the LORD (R) ... live in their own homes again (R)
decisions.reason: The formula as set for the prophets. Readable adds "again" to show that this is a return (m2).
